questions.explanation: All matter, energy, and space; includes stars, planets, gas, dust, and empty space.
A huge collection of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity.
A galaxy that is round or oval-shaped.
A galaxy shaped like a pinwheel with curved arms.
A galaxy that does not fit the spiral or elliptical categories.
The spiral galaxy that contains our solar system.
A huge ball of gas held together by gravity that gives off light and energy.
A group of stars formed at the same time and place and held together by gravity.
A recognized pattern of stars in the sky.
The Sun and the objects that orbit it, including planets, moons, asteroids, and comets.
A body that orbits the Sun, is round from its own gravity, and dominates its neighbourhood.
A natural object that orbits a planet.
A small rocky body revolving around the Sun.
A ball of rock and ice that orbits the Sun and can develop a glowing tail when heated.
A unit of distance equal to how far light travels in one year.
About 300,000 kilometres per second.
About 9.46 trillion kilometres.
The average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres.
Distance between planets, often measured in kilometres or AU.
Distance between stars within a galaxy, usually measured in light-years.
Distance between galaxies, usually measured in light-years.
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 instead of being counted as the ninth planet.
The theory that the universe began with a rapid expansion of matter and radiation.
According to the Big Bang Theory, space and time started with the initial expansion.
Soon after the Big Bang, energy changed into particles and anti-particles such as electrons and positrons.
Hydrogen and helium nuclei formed within minutes after the Big Bang.
Millions of years after the Big Bang, stars and galaxies began to form.
Stars produced the other elements through reactions in their interiors.
A change in wavelength and frequency caused by motion between a source and an observer.
Wavelengths get compressed and frequency increases.
Wavelengths stretch out and frequency decreases.
Light shifted toward lower frequencies, showing an object is moving away.
Light shifted toward higher frequencies, showing an object is moving closer.
The astronomer who used Doppler evidence in the 1920s to show the universe is expanding.
The idea that space itself is stretching, increasing the distance between galaxies.
Galaxies are generally red-shifted and the farther they are, the faster they move away.
Microwave radiation found throughout the universe and interpreted as afterglow from the Big Bang.
Another way to describe the cosmic microwave background radiation.
Since 1965, scientists have observed microwave radiation filling the universe.
It supports the idea that leftover energy from the early universe is still present today.
Stars can be described by colour, temperature, and absolute magnitude.
An object that bends light and separates it into individual colours.
An instrument that splits incoming light into a spectrum.
The band or series of colours produced when light is separated.
Light from a star reveals information about its properties.
A substance made of only one kind of atom.
Each element gives off a distinct colour pattern when heated.
Astronomers use spectra to identify which elements are present in stars.
A star’s colour is linked to how hot or cool it is.
A cooler star compared with blue or blue-white stars.
A hotter star than a red star.
Stars may look white to the eye but show different colours through binoculars or telescopes.
The long sequence of stages from a star’s birth to its later changes.
A star forms when gas and dust collapse and conditions allow fusion to begin.
The process that powers stars by combining lighter nuclei into heavier ones.
Their life cycles are so long that they appear unchanged in the night sky.
The most accepted theory that the solar system formed from the collapse of a cloud of gas and dust.
A cloud of dust and gas in space.
About 5 billion years ago.
The inward pull that caused the nebula to shrink and form the solar system.
As the nebula collapsed, it flattened into a rotating disk.
The forming young Sun at the centre of the solar nebula.
Clumps of matter that were still condensing and later became planets.
Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars; small rocky terrestrial planets.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune; large Jovian planets.
They formed in different parts of the nebula where temperatures were different.
Close to the Sun, ices vaporized and mostly rock and metal could condense.
Farther from the Sun, ices and gases could condense to build giant planets.
Small rocky planets formed in the hotter inner solar system.
Large gas-rich planets formed in the colder outer solar system.
Natural satellites that formed or were captured during solar system development.
Leftover smaller bodies from the formation of the solar system.
Distance from the Sun affected temperature, which affected what materials could condense.
An ordinary yellow dwarf star and the closest star to Earth.
It controls Earth’s climate and weather and sustains life.
The Sun contains over 99.8% of the mass of the solar system.
The Sun’s outer layers that we can observe.
The visible surface layer of the Sun.
A transparent layer above the photosphere.
The outermost transparent layer of the Sun’s atmosphere.
The central region of the Sun where energy is produced.
The process in the Sun’s core that changes hydrogen into helium and releases huge amounts of energy.
Energy moves from the core to outer layers and is radiated as heat, ultraviolet rays, and x-rays.
A cooler, darker area on the Sun’s visible surface caused by magnetic activity.
A repeating pattern in sunspot activity over time.
A sudden release of magnetic energy from the Sun’s corona.
They can disrupt electrical power and communications on Earth.
A 1989 solar flare caused a power outage across Quebec for more than nine hours.
An eruption of gas from the chromosphere forming columns or loops.
Some prominences stay arched because magnetic fields hold them up.
A stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun.
A telescope that collects and focuses visible light to magnify distant objects.
Using ground-based tools such as telescopes to study space.
Using satellites, probes, and orbiting observatories above Earth’s atmosphere.
Anything that orbits something else.
A naturally orbiting body such as the Moon.
A human-made object placed in orbit, such as communication satellites around Earth.
An unpiloted device sent to another celestial body to collect information.
They are usually less costly and less dangerous than sending humans.
Non-functioning satellites and debris orbiting Earth.
An orbiting observatory that collects detailed images and data from space.
A large permanently occupied orbiting laboratory used for research and technology development.
A stepping-stone for future space exploration and a platform for scientific study.
A spacecraft mission that explored Saturn and its rings, ending in 2017.
A robotic rover exploring Mars to gather scientific data.
A NASA spacecraft designed to study the Sun up close.
To gather close-up data about solar wind and solar activity.
The Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth over fifty years ago.
Different cultures use stories, observation, and traditions to understand the sky.
Astronomy is often seen as one of the oldest sciences.
People used the sky to guide travel, tell time, and understand seasons.
Observing the sky helped people predict seasonal change and plan farming activities.
Stories created by cultures to explain the origin of the universe and Earth.
A tradition that mainly studies the physical realm of the world.
They add both physical knowledge and broader perspectives to our understanding of the universe.
A First Peoples of North America oral story in which mud is brought from primeval water to form Earth.
The being in the Earth Diver story who dives or sends animals to bring back mud.
The Morning Star in an oral story from Arnhem Land in Australia.
The Island of the Dead where Barnumbir lives in the story.
An Australian First Peoples story linking Venus and cultural understanding of the sky.
The study and travel beyond Earth, including scientific, technical, and ethical issues.
Astronauts face dangers because technology can fail and space is a harsh environment.
A space shuttle disaster in 1986 often used as an example of spaceflight risk.
A space shuttle disaster in 2003 showing the dangers of space travel.
Orbiting debris from human space activity that can damage spacecraft.
Even a tiny speck of paint can seriously damage a shuttle or probe in a collision.
Commercial companies are increasingly involved in launching and carrying people or payloads into space.
Paying for a trip into space or near-space as a private customer.
A company planning sub-orbital tourist flights to about 100 kilometres above Earth.
A company known for arranging private spaceflight opportunities.
Changing another planet’s environment to make it more like Earth.
It may drive the development of new technologies.
Space-related projects require major investment in science and technology.
People debate whether limited public money should be spent on space projects.
Issues in space exploration often involve ethics, environment, and politics.
Space exploration issues are complex and do not fit neatly into only good or bad categories.
